topic.subject: social
topic.title: Globalisation and the Indian economy
topic.scope: MNCs, foreign trade, liberalisation, WTO, impact on producers and workers, fair globalisation

misconceptions.statement: MNCs only produce goods in their home country.
misconceptions.why: Students assume a company's identity is tied strictly to its country of origin.
misconceptions.fix: MNCs set up production units in countries where labor is cheap and resources are available to maximize profit.

probe.question: Where does a US-based MNC produce its goods?

misconceptions.root_belief: A brand's origin dictates its entire operational geography.

misconceptions.statement: Removing trade barriers always helps every local producer.
misconceptions.why: Students equate 'free trade' with 'fair trade' for everyone.
misconceptions.fix: Removing barriers allows cheaper imports, which can force small, less efficient local producers out of business.

probe.question: What happens to small toy makers when trade barriers are removed?
probe.wrong_answer: They sell more because of global competition

misconceptions.root_belief: Competition is always beneficial for all participants.

misconceptions.statement: The WTO is a democratic body where all countries have equal power.
misconceptions.why: Students assume international organizations function like national parliaments.
misconceptions.fix: The WTO is dominated by developed countries that often force developing nations to follow rules that favor the rich.

probe.question: Does the WTO treat all member countries equally?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is a democratic global parliament

misconceptions.root_belief: International organizations are inherently neutral and fair.

misconceptions.statement: Globalisation is a natural process that cannot be changed by government policy.
misconceptions.why: Students view globalisation as a technological inevitability rather than a political choice.
misconceptions.fix: Globalisation is shaped by government policies; fair globalisation can be achieved through better labor laws and support for small producers.

probe.question: Can the government make globalisation fairer?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is a global market force beyond control

misconceptions.root_belief: Economic forces are laws of nature.

misconceptions.statement: An MNC owns and runs all its factories itself in every country.
misconceptions.why: Students see big brand names and assume direct ownership everywhere, missing partnerships and contracts.
misconceptions.fix: MNCs often set up production by buying local companies, partnering with them, or placing orders with small local producers who supply goods at low prices.

probe.question: A large foreign brand gets its garments made in India by small local factories under orders. Who owns those factories?

misconceptions.root_belief: Companies must own everything they sell
misconceptions.source_hint: NCERT Class 10 Economics Ch.4 text and classroom discussion

misconceptions.statement: MNCs set up factories in a country mainly to help that country's people get jobs.
misconceptions.why: Students link foreign investment with job creation and ignore the company's own profit motive.
misconceptions.fix: MNCs set up production where costs of labour and other inputs are low and markets are close, so as to earn more profit; jobs are a side effect.

probe.question: Why does an MNC choose to set up a factory in a particular region of India?
probe.wrong_answer: To provide employment to the people there.

misconceptions.root_belief: Companies invest mainly to help the host country

misconceptions.statement: Production across countries means a product is made completely in one place and then shipped abroad.
misconceptions.why: Students think of trade as only exchange of finished goods and not of production spread in stages.
misconceptions.fix: Production is split into parts made in different countries, where each stage is done at the place with the lowest cost, and then assembled.

probe.question: A phone's design is in one country, parts in another and assembly in a third. What is this called?
probe.wrong_answer: Ordinary export of a finished good.

misconceptions.root_belief: Goods are produced wholly in one place

misconceptions.statement: Foreign trade only means exporting goods from a country to other countries.
misconceptions.why: Students notice exports in news and forget imports are also part of trade.
misconceptions.fix: Foreign trade includes both exports and imports; it links markets of different countries and gives buyers more choice of goods.

probe.question: When Indian shops sell imported Chinese toys, does this show integration with foreign markets?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because trade means only selling Indian goods abroad.

misconceptions.statement: Foreign trade gives benefits only to the producers, not to consumers.
misconceptions.why: Students think of trade as business activity and overlook what buyers gain.
misconceptions.fix: Foreign trade gives consumers more choice and often lower prices, while producers get a wider market to sell in.

probe.question: After imports of goods began, what changed for Indian consumers?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing changed for consumers; only producers gained.

misconceptions.statement: Trade barriers like import tax were removed in India because the WTO forced the country to do so in 1947.
misconceptions.why: Students mix the dates and the agents of reform, joining WTO and liberalisation together.
misconceptions.fix: India removed many trade barriers from 1991 as part of its own liberalisation policy; a tax on imports is a trade barrier and quotas also limit imports.

probe.question: When did India begin removing many trade barriers like import tax and quotas?

misconceptions.root_belief: Trade reforms came from outside at independence

misconceptions.statement: After liberalisation, Indian small producers all became bigger and richer through competition.
misconceptions.why: Students take the word competition as always leading to growth and ignore weaker firms.
misconceptions.fix: Competition has helped some Indian companies grow, but many small producers, such as in batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys and vegetable oil, had to shut down or lose jobs.

probe.question: What happened to many small Indian toy makers when cheap imports came in?
probe.wrong_answer: They all grew bigger and earned more.

misconceptions.statement: Fair globalisation means every country should open its markets the same amount.
misconceptions.why: Students equate fairness with identical treatment and ignore differences in the capacity of rich and poor countries.
misconceptions.fix: Fair globalisation creates opportunities for all and ensures benefits are shared better; rules should protect the weak, and developed countries should also cut their own trade barriers.

probe.question: What would make globalisation fair for developing countries?
probe.wrong_answer: Every country, rich or poor, opening its markets equally.

misconceptions.root_belief: Fairness means identical rules for all
